## What this is for

The Grit-O scale was written around two facets of grit, perseverance of effort and consistency of interest. Does it measure one thing or two? [Factor analysis I](fa-exploratory.qmd) let the data propose a structure. This lesson states a structure first and asks whether the data agree: **confirmatory factor analysis** (CFA). A written-down structure also answers three more questions. How well does it fit? How reliable is a score built on it (**omega**)? And what is it, seen from item response theory? Each fit also needs an **estimator**, and we choose one out loud for both of our scales. Along the way we settle whether the DASS-21 yields one score or three.

## Goals

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

- write a confirmatory factor model in `lavaan` syntax, say how it is identified, and count its degrees of freedom;
- read χ², CFI, TLI, RMSEA and SRMR, say what each responds to, and compare nested models;
- compute omega and omega hierarchical, and say when omega equals alpha;
- convert an ordinal factor loading and threshold into a slope and a difficulty, and check the conversion against `mirt`;
- choose an estimator (ML, MLR or WLSMV) and a treatment of missing responses from what the data look like.

## Core ideas

### Stating the structure first

A confirmatory model is the common factor model with most loadings fixed at zero before the data are seen. For grit, perseverance items load on one factor and consistency items on the other, with each item's other loading fixed at 0. [Jöreskog (1969)](https://doi.org/10.1007/bf02289343) showed how to fit such a model by maximum likelihood and test it. We use the `lavaan` package ([Rosseel, 2012](https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v048.i02)), whose syntax reads almost like a path diagram. `=~` means "is measured by", and an item left off a line has its loading on that factor fixed at zero:

```r
two <- "per =~ g1 + g4 + g6 + g9 + g10 + g12
        con =~ g2 + g3 + g5 + g7 + g8 + g11"
fit <- cfa(two, data = grit)
```

The factors may correlate (lavaan's default), and each item keeps a unique variance.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**Recall** from [Factor analysis I](fa-exploratory.qmd): with two or more factors, any rotation reproduces the correlations exactly as well as any other. The data fix the correlations, not the frame of the factors.
:::

The zeros pin the frame, since rotating would move them. One indeterminacy is left: a factor has no natural unit. The model is identified once each factor's scale is set, by fixing one loading per factor to 1 (lavaan's default) or each factor's variance to 1 (`std.lv = TRUE`). The two choices fit identically and report loadings in different units, as the grit output shows.

What can the data test? They supply $p(p+1)/2$ variances and covariances. The model spends one parameter on each free loading, unique variance and factor correlation. The **degrees of freedom** are the difference, and each one is a constraint the data could violate.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
quiz({
  q: "Twelve items, two factors, each item loading on one factor only, factor variances fixed at 1 and the factors correlated. How many degrees of freedom does the model have?",
  options: [
    {text: "53", correct: true, why: "There are $12 \\times 13/2 = 78$ variances and covariances. The model estimates 12 loadings, 12 unique variances and 1 factor correlation, 25 in all: $78 - 25 = 53$."},
    {text: "54", correct: false, why: "That is the one-factor model, with 24 parameters. The factor correlation costs one more."},
    {text: "66", correct: false, why: "That counts only the 66 covariances and forgets the 12 variances the data also supply."}
  ]
})
```

### Fit indices, and what they can't tell you

Every fit index compares the covariance matrix the model implies with the one the data supply. The likelihood-ratio **χ²** tests exact fit: it is $N - 1$ times the discrepancy, so a large sample rejects any model that is slightly wrong, and every model is. The other indices ask how wrong. **RMSEA** is the misfit per degree of freedom ([Steiger, 1990](https://doi.org/10.1207/s15327906mbr2502_4)). **CFI** ([Bentler, 1990](https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.107.2.238)) and **TLI** ([Tucker & Lewis, 1973](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02291170)) compare the model's misfit with that of a baseline in which the items are uncorrelated. **SRMR** is the root mean square residual correlation.

[Hu and Bentler (1999)](https://doi.org/10.1080/10705519909540118) found, in simulations of maximum-likelihood estimation, that cutoffs near 0.95 for CFI and TLI, 0.06 for RMSEA and 0.08 for SRMR were needed to call a fit good. [Marsh, Hau and Wen (2004)](https://doi.org/10.1207/s15328007sem1103_2) argue against reading them as fixed rules, and with ordinal estimators the same indices tell a different story ([Xia & Yang, 2019](https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-018-1055-2)). They describe how far off a model is; the residuals show where.

#### Try it: what misfit does to fit indices

Six items, two factors correlated 0.3. The population also has things the model leaves out: item 3 loads on the second factor, and items 5 and 6 share an error. The widget fits the two-factor model by maximum likelihood.

```{ojs}

viewof fs_cross = Inputs.range([0, 0.5], {value: 0.3, step: 0.05, label: "Item 3's loading on factor 2 (not in the model)"})
viewof fs_cerr = Inputs.range([0, 0.3], {value: 0, step: 0.05, label: "Error covariance, items 5 and 6 (not in the model)"})
viewof fs_n = Inputs.range([100, 5000], {value: 500, step: 100, label: "Sample size N"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false

  const lam = [0.7, 0.6, 0.5, 0.7, 0.6, 0.5];
  const L = lam.map((v, i) => i < 3 ? [v, 0] : [0, v]); L[2][1] = fs_cross;
  const P = [[1, 0.3], [0.3, 1]];
  const common = implied(L, P, zeros(6));
  const Th = zeros(6).map((r, i) => r.map((_, j) => i === j ? 1 - common[i][i] : 0));
  Th[4][5] = Th[5][4] = fs_cerr;

  return {S, fit, idx: fitIndices(S, fit, 13, fs_n)};
}
fs_res = fs.S.flatMap((r, i) => r.map((v, j) => ({row: `Item ${i + 1}`, col: `Item ${j + 1}`, res: v - fs.fit.Sigma[i][j]})))
Plot.plot({
  width: 400, height: 380, padding: 0.04, x: {label: null, axis: "top"}, y: {label: null},

  marks: [Plot.cell(fs_res, {x: "col", y: "row", fill: "res"}),
          Plot.text(fs_res, {x: "col", y: "row", text: d => d.res.toFixed(2), fontSize: 12, fill: palette.ink})]

```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
md`Expected χ² **${fs.idx.chisq.toFixed(1)}** on ${fs.idx.df} df (the 5% critical value is 15.5) · CFI **${fs.idx.cfi.toFixed(3)}** · RMSEA **${fs.idx.rmsea.toFixed(3)}** · SRMR **${fs.idx.srmr.toFixed(3)}** · estimated factor correlation **${fs.fit.Phi[0][1].toFixed(2)}** (true 0.3)`
```

At the start, the omitted cross-loading gives an RMSEA of 0.080 and a CFI of 0.944, and the factor correlation comes out at 0.48: the model routes item 3's link to factor 2 through the correlation. The residuals point at item 3. Move N from 500 to 2,000: χ² rises from 34 to 111, and the other indices stay put. Now set the cross-loading to 0 and the error covariance to 0.2. CFI is 0.994 and RMSEA 0.026, inside the cutoffs, and the residual for items 5 and 6 is almost zero: the model raised their loadings to absorb the shared error, and the strain shows up between item 4 and items 1–3. A residual marks where the model strains, which isn't always where the cause is.

Nested models can be compared directly: the one-factor model is the two-factor model with the factor correlation fixed at 1, so the difference in χ² tests that constraint. Robust estimators need a scaled difference ([Satorra & Bentler, 2001](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02296192)), which `lavTestLRT()` computes. Prediction offers another view: [Zhang et al. ### Omega: reliability from the model

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**Recall** from [Classical test theory and reliability](ctt-reliability.qmd): alpha is a lower bound on reliability, with equality under essential tau-equivalence. [Factor analysis I](fa-exploratory.qmd) read tau-equivalence as a one-factor model with equal loadings.
:::

A factor model makes the bound unnecessary. Under a one-factor model with loadings $\lambda_i$ and unique variances $\psi_i$, the sum score has variance $(\sum_i \lambda_i)^2 + \sum_i \psi_i$, of which $(\sum_i\lambda_i)^2$ comes from the factor. Their ratio is **omega** ([McDonald, 1999](https://doi.org/10.4324/9781410601087)):
$$\omega = \frac{(\sum_i \lambda_i)^2}{(\sum_i \lambda_i)^2 + \sum_i \psi_i}.$$
When the loadings are equal, omega equals alpha (problem 1). When they aren't, alpha is smaller, usually by a little ([Revelle & Zinbarg, 2009](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11336-008-9102-z)).

Omega raises a sharper question when a scale has subscales. In a **bifactor** model ([Holzinger & Swineford, 1937](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02287965); [Reise, 2012](https://doi.org/10.1080/00273171.2012.715555)), every item loads on a general factor and on one specific factor for its subscale, with all factors uncorrelated. **Omega total** counts the general and specific factors as signal. **Omega hierarchical**, $\omega_h$, counts only the general factor: it is the share of the total score's variance that one common construct accounts for ([Rodriguez, Reise & Haviland, 2016](https://doi.org/10.1037/met0000045)).

#### Try it: alpha, omega and omega hierarchical

Nine items in three subscales of three.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof om_g = Inputs.range([0.3, 0.6], {value: 0.6, step: 0.05, label: "Average general-factor loading"})
viewof om_sp = Inputs.range([0, 0.3], {value: 0, step: 0.05, label: "Spread of general loadings (± within each subscale)"})
viewof om_s = Inputs.range([0, 0.4], {value: 0, step: 0.05, label: "Specific-factor loading"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
om = {
  const off = [-1, 0, 1, -1, 0, 1, -1, 0, 1];
  return omegas(off.map(o => om_g + om_sp * o), off.map(() => om_s), [1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3]);
}
om_rows = [{k: "Alpha", v: om.alpha}, {k: "Omega total", v: om.omegaT}, {k: "Omega hierarchical", v: om.omegaH}]
Plot.plot({
  width: 560, height: 170, marginLeft: 150, x: {domain: [0, 1], label: "Coefficient"}, y: {label: null, domain: om_rows.map(d => d.k)},
  marks: [Plot.barX(om_rows, {y: "k", x: "v", fill: d => d.k === "Alpha" ? palette.contrast : palette.main}),
          Plot.text(om_rows, {y: "k", x: "v", text: d => d.v.toFixed(3), dx: 22})]
})
```

With equal loadings and no specific factors, all three are 0.835. Spread the loadings to ±0.2 and alpha falls a little below omega (0.833 against 0.841): the lower bound at work. Set the spread to 0 and the specific loading to 0.4: omega total rises to 0.886 and omega hierarchical falls to 0.771, because the subscales now carry reliable variance of their own. Alpha sits between the two.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
quiz({
  q: "A scale's bifactor model gives $\\omega_{\\text{total}} = 0.90$ and $\\omega_h = 0.80$. How is the variance of its total score divided?",
  options: [
    {text: "80% general factor, 10% specific factors, 10% unique", correct: true, why: "$\\omega_h$ is the general factor's share; $\\omega_{\\text{total}} - \\omega_h = 0.10$ is the specific factors' share; the remaining $1 - 0.90$ is unique variance."},
    {text: "90% general factor, 10% unique", correct: false, why: "That would make $\\omega_h = \\omega_{\\text{total}}$. The 0.10 gap between them belongs to the specific factors."},
    {text: "80% general factor, 20% unique", correct: false, why: "The specific factors are reliable variance too; omega total counts them, which is why it is 0.90."}
  ]
})
```

### Item response theory as factor analysis

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**Recall** from [From the 1PL to the 4PL](1pl-to-4pl.qmd): the 2PL gives each item a slope $a$ and a difficulty $b$; `mirt` writes $a\theta + d$, so $b = -d/a$.
:::

[Factor analysis I](fa-exploratory.qmd) treated an ordered response as a coarsened continuous one and factored polychoric correlations. Write that down for one item: a latent response $y^* = \lambda\eta + \varepsilon$, with $\text{var}(y^*) = 1$, and $x = 1$ when $y^*$ passes a threshold $\tau$. Then
$$\Pr(x = 1 \mid \eta) = \Phi\!\left(\frac{\lambda\eta - \tau}{\sqrt{1 - \lambda^2}}\right) = \Phi\big(a(\eta - b)\big), \quad a = \frac{\lambda}{\sqrt{1-\lambda^2}},\; b = \frac{\tau}{\lambda}.$$
That is the normal-ogive 2PL. The factor model for dichotomous items *is* an item response model ([Takane & de Leeuw, 1987](https://doi.org/10.1007/bf02294363)), and with more categories each threshold becomes a category boundary of the graded response model ([Samejima, 1969](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF03372160); [Kamata & Bauer, 2008](https://doi.org/10.1080/10705510701758406)). For the logistic metric of `mirt` ([Chalmers, 2012](https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v048.i06)) and this course, multiply the slope by about 1.7 ([Camilli, 1994](https://doi.org/10.3102/10769986019003293), on where the constant comes from); this is the only place in the course it appears.

#### Try it: loading to slope

```{ojs}

viewof ls_l = Inputs.range([0.1, 0.95], {value: 0.7, step: 0.05, label: "Loading λ"})
viewof ls_t = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: 0.35, step: 0.05, label: "Threshold τ"})
```

```{ojs}

  const irt = ogiveToIRT(ls_l, ls_t);
  const g = grid(-4, 4, 161);
  const maxDiff = Math.max(...g.map(e => Math.abs(pOgive(e, ls_l, ls_t) - p2plAB(e, irt.a, irt.b))));
  return {irt, maxDiff, rows: g.flatMap(e => [
    {eta: e, p: pOgive(e, ls_l, ls_t), curve: "Factor model (normal ogive)"},
    {eta: e, p: p2plAB(e, irt.a, irt.b), curve: "Logistic 2PL, a = 1.702 × normal slope"}])};
}
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 300, x: {label: "Factor η (= θ)"}, y: {label: "Pr(x = 1)", domain: [0, 1]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Factor model (normal ogive)", "Logistic 2PL, a = 1.702 × normal slope"], range: [palette.main, palette.contrast]},
  marks: [Plot.ruleX([ls.irt.b], {stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
          Plot.line(ls.rows, {x: "eta", y: "p", stroke: "curve", strokeWidth: 2.5})]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
md`Normal-ogive slope **${ls.irt.aNormal.toFixed(2)}**, logistic slope **${ls.irt.a.toFixed(2)}**, difficulty b = τ/λ = **${ls.irt.b.toFixed(2)}** (dashed line). Largest gap between the two curves: **${ls.maxDiff.toFixed(3)}**.`
```

At a loading of 0.7 and a threshold of 0.35, the slope is 0.98 (normal ogive) or 1.67 (logistic), the difficulty is 0.5, and the curves never differ by more than 0.01, wherever the sliders sit. Push the loading to 0.9 and the slope passes 3.5; at 0.95 it passes 5. Loadings stop at 1 and slopes don't.

## Go deeper: ordinal factor analysis is the graded response model

**Assumptions:** an item with ordered categories $0, \dots, K$; a latent response $y^* = \lambda^\top \eta + \varepsilon$ with $\eta$ multivariate normal (variances 1), $\varepsilon \sim N(0, 1 - h^2)$ independent of $\eta$ and of the other items' errors, where $h^2 = \text{var}(\lambda^\top\eta)$ is the communality, so $\text{var}(y^*) = 1$. The response is $x = k$ when $\tau_k < y^* \le \tau_{k+1}$, with $\tau_0 = -\infty$ and $\tau_{K+1} = \infty$.

**Boundary curves.** For $k = 1, \dots, K$,
$$\Pr(x \ge k \mid \eta) = \Pr(\varepsilon > \tau_k - \lambda^\top\eta) = \Phi\!\left(\frac{\lambda^\top\eta - \tau_k}{\sqrt{1 - h^2}}\right).$$
With one factor this is $\Phi\big(a(\eta - b_k)\big)$ with $a = \lambda/\sqrt{1-\lambda^2}$ and $b_k = \tau_k/\lambda$: one slope per item and one boundary per category, which is Samejima's (1969) normal-ogive graded response model. Category probabilities are differences of adjacent boundary curves. With several factors, the slope on factor $m$ is $a_m = \lambda_m/\sqrt{1 - h^2}$.

**Local independence.** The errors are independent across items, so given $\eta$ the responses are independent. Item response theory's local independence is the factor model's uncorrelated unique parts.

**Logistic metric.** $\sup_z |\Phi(z) - \text{logit}^{-1}(1.702z)| < 0.01$ (the widget's gap), so a logistic slope is about $1.702a$; in `mirt`'s form, $d_k = -1.702\,a\,b_k$.

**Why the numbers differ in practice.** The model is the same; the estimators are not. `lavaan`'s WLSMV estimates thresholds and polychoric correlations, which use the data one or two items at a time ([Muthén, 1984](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02294210); [Flora & Curran, 2004](https://doi.org/10.1037/1082-989X.9.4.466)). `mirt` maximizes the likelihood of whole response patterns. When the model holds they converge on the same values as the sample grows; in a finite sample they differ by sampling error, by the logistic approximation, and wherever the model misfits, since the two estimators weigh the misfit differently.
:::

### Choosing an estimator

Which estimator should a fit use? That depends on the categories and how they are used, the distance from normality, the sample size and what is missing. Three of `lavaan`'s estimators ([tutorial](https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/est.html)) cover most scales.

- **ML** (maximum likelihood), the default for numeric data, treats the items as continuous and multivariate normal ([Li, 2016](https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-015-0619-7)).
- **MLR** keeps the ML estimates and makes the standard errors and the χ² robust to non-normality ([Yuan & Bentler, 2000](https://doi.org/10.1111/0081-1750.00078); [Savalei, 2014](https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2013.824793), on how the corrections work).
- **WLSMV**, `lavaan`'s choice when items are declared `ordered`, fits the ordinal model of the previous section to thresholds and polychoric correlations by diagonally weighted least squares ([Muthén, 1984](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02294210); [lavaan tutorial, "Categorical data"](https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/cat.html)). It assumes normal latent responses, not normal observed ones, and tolerates modest departures from that ([Flora & Curran, 2004](https://doi.org/10.1037/1082-989X.9.4.466)).

`lavaan` drops incomplete respondents by default; with ML or MLR, `missing = "ml"` gives **full-information ML** (FIML), which uses every observed response. With responses missing at random ([Rubin, 1976](https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/63.3.581)), FIML was unbiased and more efficient than listwise or pairwise deletion in the simulations of [Enders and Bandalos (2001)](https://doi.org/10.1207/S15328007SEM0803_5). WLSMV has no FIML in `lavaan`; for ordered items, the full-information route is the same model as a graded response model in `mirt` ([Bock & Aitkin, 1981](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02293801)).

When do they part ways? In simulations by [Rhemtulla, Brosseau-Liard and Savalei (2012)](https://doi.org/10.1037/a0029315), the categorical estimator recovered loadings and standard errors better, especially with fewer than five categories, and robust ML did as well on factor correlations and fit; ML was the more sensitive to asymmetric thresholds, the categorical estimator to small samples and non-normal latent responses. With two or three categories, WLSMV's χ² held its nominal rejection rate better ([Beauducel & Herzberg, 2006](https://doi.org/10.1207/s15328007sem1302_2)). [Li (2016)](https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-015-0619-7) found WLSMV's loadings less biased almost everywhere, but MLR's standard errors better in small samples with non-normal latent responses. As a guide:

| The responses | A reasonable first choice | In `lavaan` |
|---|---|---|
| Continuous, roughly normal | ML | the default |
| Continuous but skewed, or five or more categories used fairly evenly | MLR | `estimator = "MLR"` |
| Fewer than five categories, or piled at one end | WLSMV | `ordered = TRUE` |
| Some responses missing | FIML with ML or MLR; with WLSMV, pairwise deletion or the graded model in `mirt` | `missing = "ml"` or `"pairwise"` |
| A few hundred respondents or fewer | MLR with five or more categories; else WLSMV, checked against MLR | |

The target matters too: omega is about the sum of the scored responses, so it needs a model of those responses even when the structure is fitted to polychorics. Fit a second reasonable estimator as a check; where two defensible choices disagree, the choice matters for these data.

## Simulate

The code simulates 1,000 respondents answering eight four-category items from two correlated factors, fits the CFA with `lavaan` and the graded model with `mirt`, and puts both on the logistic IRT scale. The first run takes 20–30 seconds.

With the seed as written, every slope from either route is within 0.3 of the truth, and the factor correlation comes out at 0.36 (true 0.4). Set `np <- 300` and the slopes scatter; with 5,000 respondents they settle.


::: {.cell}
```{webr}
#| results: markup
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| include: true
#| label: unnamed-chunk-16
# Simulate ordinal responses from a two-factor model, fit a confirmatory factor
# analysis with lavaan and a graded response model with mirt, and compare both
# with the truth on the IRT scale. Needs the lavaan and mirt packages.
library(lavaan)
library(mirt)
set.seed(59)
np  <- 1000                                   # respondents (try 300, or 5000 locally)
lam <- c(0.8, 0.7, 0.6, 0.5, 0.8, 0.7, 0.6, 0.5)   # loadings: items 1-4 on F1, 5-8 on F2
phi <- 0.4                                    # correlation between the factors
tau <- c(-1, 0, 1)                            # thresholds that cut y* into 0, 1, 2, 3

# Latent responses y* = loading * factor + error, with var(y*) = 1; then cut.
eta <- matrix(rnorm(np * 2), np) %*% chol(matrix(c(1, phi, phi, 1), 2))
f   <- rep(1:2, each = 4)
ystar <- sapply(1:8, function(i) lam[i] * eta[, f[i]] + sqrt(1 - lam[i]^2) * rnorm(np))
resp <- as.data.frame(apply(ystar, 2, function(y) findInterval(y, tau)))
names(resp) <- paste0("x", 1:8)

# The CFA, on polychoric correlations (items declared ordered).
fit <- cfa("F1 =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4
            F2 =~ x5 + x6 + x7 + x8", data = resp, ordered = TRUE, std.lv = TRUE)
lam_hat <- rowSums(lavInspect(fit, "std")$lambda)

# The graded response model in mirt, one factor at a time. Each item loads on one
# factor, so this estimates the same slopes as a two-dimensional fit, which takes
# minutes in the browser (change it to mirt.model("F1 = 1-4 / F2 = 5-8 / COV = F1*F2",
# on three lines, to try it locally).
a_mirt <- c(coef(mirt(resp[1:4], 1, itemtype = "graded", verbose = FALSE), simplify = TRUE)$items[, "a1"],
            coef(mirt(resp[5:8], 1, itemtype = "graded", verbose = FALSE), simplify = TRUE)$items[, "a1"])

# On the logistic IRT scale: a = 1.702 * lambda / sqrt(1 - lambda^2).
to_a <- function(l) 1.702 * l / sqrt(1 - l^2)
print(round(data.frame(true_loading = lam, cfa_loading = lam_hat,
                       true_a = to_a(lam), a_from_cfa = to_a(lam_hat), a_mirt = a_mirt), 2))
cat("factor correlation: true", phi, " lavaan", round(lavInspect(fit, "cor.lv")[1, 2], 2), "\n")
print(round(fitMeasures(fit, c("chisq.scaled", "df", "cfi.scaled", "rmsea.scaled")), 3))

```

### Grit: one factor or two?

Our main example is [grit](https://itemresponsewarehouse.org/tables/grit/): the 12 items of the Grit-O ([Duckworth, Peterson, Matthews & Kelly, 2007](https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.92.6.1087)), answered online through [Open Psychometrics](https://openpsychometrics.org/_rawdata/). Its job is to test a designed two-facet structure. [Download the code](code/fa-confirmatory-irw.R) to run every chunk.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="show"}
library(lavaan)
# Each IRW table has a landing page (itemresponsewarehouse.org/tables/<name>/)
# with a CSV download. This link is pinned to one version of the data.
grit_url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse:v59_0.grit/rows?format=csv"
df <- read.csv(grit_url)
wide <- tapply(df$resp, list(df$id, df$item), function(x) x[1])
grit_all <- as.data.frame(wide[, paste0("item_", 1:12)])
names(grit_all) <- paste0("g", 1:12)
grit_all <- grit_all[rowSums(!is.na(grit_all)) > 0, ]   # drop respondents with no responses
# Keying. The source (Open Psychometrics) coded 1 = "Very much like me" to
# 5 = "Not like me at all", and the IRW processing script reversed the six
# consistency-of-interest items (2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 11), which are worded against grit.
# So every item in the table runs toward LESS grit. Reversing all twelve makes
# higher = more grit, the same as reversing the perseverance items in the raw data.
grit_all <- 6 - grit_all
grit <- grit_all[complete.cases(grit_all), ]
per <- paste0("g", c(1, 4, 6, 9, 10, 12))   # perseverance of effort
con <- paste0("g", c(2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 11))    # consistency of interest
round(range(cor(grit)[lower.tri(diag(12))]), 2)   # no negative correlations left
```

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="show"}
bi <- cfa(mbi, data = dass, estimator = "MLR", std.lv = TRUE, orthogonal = TRUE)
L <- lavInspect(bi, "est")$lambda
th <- diag(lavInspect(bi, "est")$theta)
total_var <- sum(colSums(L)^2) + sum(th)
omega_h_sub <- c(dep = sum(L[dep, "dep"])^2 / (sum(colSums(L[dep, ])^2) + sum(th[dep])),
                 anx = sum(L[anx, "anx"])^2 / (sum(colSums(L[anx, ])^2) + sum(th[anx])),
                 str = sum(L[stress, "str"])^2 / (sum(colSums(L[stress, ])^2) + sum(th[stress])))
round(c(omega_total = sum(colSums(L)^2) / total_var,
        omega_hierarchical = sum(L[, "distress"])^2 / total_var,
        alpha = alpha(dass)), 3)
```

Omega total is 0.944 and omega hierarchical 0.879: one general factor accounts for almost all of the total score's reliable variance. Within each scale, the specific factor's share of the scale score is 0.24 for depression, 0.23 for anxiety and 0.002 for stress; the stress items carry almost nothing beyond general distress.

Should a clinic report three DASS scores or one? The subscales add information only through their specific factors, which are small here, and the DASS authors describe the total as a sensible composite ([DASS FAQ, no. 26](https://www2.psy.unsw.edu.au/dass/DASSFAQ.htm)). For a community sample like this one, I would report the total, and the depression and anxiety scores only alongside it. A clinical sample could give a different answer. Would women and men with the same level of distress answer the DASS alike? [Measurement invariance](measurement-invariance.qmd) takes this table up there.

## Problems

1. **Omega and alpha.** Show that under a one-factor model with equal loadings $\lambda$ and equal unique variances, omega equals alpha. Then show that with unequal loadings (and uncorrelated errors) alpha is smaller.
2. **The probit link.** Starting from $y^* = \lambda\eta + \varepsilon$ with $\text{var}(y^*) = 1$, derive the normal-ogive slope and difficulty of a dichotomized item. Use your result on grit: which facet's items discriminate better, and does `mirt` agree?
3. **A patch or a finding?** (a) Run `modindices()` on the two-factor grit model; among the largest suggestions is a correlated error between items 3 and 11. Add it. How much does fit improve? Given the codebook's stems ("My interests...", "I become..."), is it a finding or a patch? Can any model of these data separate consistency of interest from wording direction ([From construct map to items](instrument-building.qmd))? (b) Dichotomize the keyed items (4 or 5 against the rest), fit the one- and two-factor binary CFAs, and compare them by the IMV ([Model fit and out-of-sample prediction](fit-prediction.qmd)) on held-out respondents with five-fold cross-validation, as [Zhang et al. (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1080/00273171.2026.2645212) do. Does prediction agree with the fit indices, item by item?
4. **Two estimators, one DASS.** Refit the three-factor DASS model with MLR and compare its standardized loadings and factor correlations with the WLSMV fit. Which move, and which way? Is that what Rhemtulla et al. (2012) and Li (2016) would lead you to expect?
5. **Design.** A new three-category scale (never, sometimes, often) will go to about 250 respondents; a pilot suggests most answers will be "never" and 1 in 10 respondents will skip an item. Which estimator and treatment of missing responses would you plan on, what would you fit as a check, and what would change your mind?
6. **Challenge (open).** [Credé, Tynan and Harms (2017)](https://doi.org/10.1037/pspp0000102) argue from a meta-analysis that grit overlaps heavily with conscientiousness. What confirmatory model would test that, and what data would you need? I don't know of a settled answer.
